sections.heading: Kamakhya Temple
sections.content: , situated in Guwahati on the Nilachal hill, is the important temple of the goddess Kali. The temples in the complex are dedicated to different forms of the mother goddess and it is an important pilgrimage. It represents the distinctive Assamese style of architecture. It is said that the female genitalia (yoni) of Lord Shivas Sati fell to the ground while he was carrying her corpse. At that instance the hill turned blue and came to be known as Nilachal (blue mountain). The temple has a beehive-like shikhara with delightful sculptured panels and images of Ganesha and other Hindu gods and goddesses on the outside. The sanctum does not have an image but a spring of water.

sections.heading: Madan Kamdev Temple
sections.content: Famous for its impressive archaeological ruins and stone sculptures, Madan Kamdev has a sculpture of Lord Shiva and the goddess Uma dating back to the Pallava dynasty (eleventh-twelfth centuries). Archaeologists also found evidence of tanks for water storage and fortifications at the site. All this shows that Madan Kamdev must have been an important town in ancient times. The wall, pillars, lintels and door frames of the temple are decorated with floral motifs, images and icons of griffins, nymphs, dancing apsaras, six headed Bhairava, four headed Shiva, women and animals in various postures.

sections.heading: Assam  Monument- Sibsagar
sections.content: Sibsagar, a historical city was the capital of the mighty Ahoms, who ruled Assam for more than six hundred years before the advent of the British. The most remarkable landmark of the town is the 200 year old Sibsagar tank. On its banks are three significant temples - Shivadol, Vishnudol and Devidol which were all built by Queen Madambika, wife of Siva Singha. The Shivadol is believed to be the highest Siva Temple in India, having a height of 104 feet and the perimeter of 195 feet. The temple belongs to the dvaikuta class in Indian temple architecture and consists of two cells  a garbhagriha (sanctum sanctorum) and a mandapa (pillared hall). The majestic shikhara (dome) with fluted vertical lines rises over the garbhagriha. Vishnudol dedicated to Lord Vishnu, has a Shiva lingam in the sanctum sanctorum, which is quite unique.

sections.heading: Museum's collections
sections.content: Established in 1940, the Assam State Museum is one of the biggest multipurpose museums in the country. With separate sections for archaeology, epigraphy, numismatics and iconography, the collection includes archaeological, wooden and bell-metal objects, ivory, terracotta, pith etc. Painting, old textiles, arms and weapons, ethnographic objects and stone sculptures are the other artifacts on display.

sections.heading: Assam  Handicrafts - Handloom
sections.content: One of the finest silk made in India is made in Assam and it is available in a wide range. Among the silk, the Muga is the most elegant which are of naturally rich golden colour. The skill to weave is seen as one of the eligibility criteria of a young girl for a marriage.

sections.heading: Assam  Handicrafts - Terracotta
sections.content: The practice of making terracottas has been flourishing throughout in Assam since ages and this craftsmanship has transmitted from one to the other. Some of the common figures start from the figures of Gods to mythological characters. The two potter communities namely the Kumhars and the Hiras are living in Assam. The Kumhars use the wheel to produce their pots but the Hiras do not use the wheel. Some of the products are earthen pot and pitchers, plates, incense stick holders and earthen lamps.

sections.heading: Assam  Handicrafts - Metal Work
sections.content: The workmanship of this craft can be found in the traditional utensils and fancy articles. Fancy articles like xorai and bota used for offering betel-nut and paan have been popular and used till now. Hajo and Sarthebari, two townships near Guwahati have the whole population working in metal. The most used metals are the bell-metal and brass.

sections.heading: Assam  Handicrafts -Toys
sections.content: Clay toys, pith, wooden and bamboo toys, cloth toys, cloth-and-mud toys are produced in Assam. Human figures like dolls and brides and grooms and a variety of animal forms are the most common forms of toys. The clay toys are in the form of gods, goddesses and other mythological figures. Clays of Pith or Indian cork made in the Goalpara region have been popular for centuries.

sections.heading: Assam - Fairs and Festivals - Bihu
sections.content: Every Assamese celebrates the festival of Bihu - there are three other main festivals which are part of Bihu namely Rangali Bihu, Bhogali Bihu and Kangali Bihu. Of all the festivals that are celebrated in Assam, the Bihu festivals are the most important one and is celebrated by all the Assamese people no matter what their caste, creed, religion and faith might be. Spring festival or Rangali celebrated in the middle of March marks the beginning of agricultural season. The Bhogali or the harvesting festival which is celebrated during January is characterized by a community feast, buffalo fight and other such entertainment. Lastly, the Kangali is another version of the festival celebrated in the middle of October marking the completion of sowing and transplanting of paddies. The festivals are characterized by songs and dance by groups of performers and observed with joy and gaiety. The performers have traditional dresses like the Dhoti, Gamccha, and Mekhala Chadar. Hips swayings, brisk steps, flinging and flipping of hands are used.

sections.heading: Assam - Fairs and Festivals - Ambubashi Mela
sections.content: This festival is dedicated to the goddess of Kamakhya and celebrated at Kamakhya temple at Guwahati. Being the centre for Tantra worship this temple attracts thousands of devotees at this annual festival during the monsoons where rituals are performed for four days.

sections.heading: Assam - Fairs and Festivals - Jonbeel Mela
sections.content: Jonbeel of Jagiroad, a township only 32 kms from Guwahati, hosts the most interesting fairs in Assam. Tribes and communities like Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi, Jaintia bring products to the fair, where they follow the traditional barter system. Traditional dances and music of each community is performed during the fair with the feeling of harmony and brotherhood among the various communities.
